title: pkg-r/NEWS.md stops at 0.1.0 while the package is at 0.2.0
description:
`pkg-r/NEWS.md` has one heading, `# plotomics 0.1.0`. `pkg-r/DESCRIPTION` is at 0.2.0, and the root
`CHANGELOG.md` covers 0.2.0 in full.

`pkg-r/README.md` links readers to the built changelog:

```
- [Changelog](https://www.samuelbharti.com/plotomics/r/news/)
```

That page is generated from `NEWS.md`, so it resolves to a changelog with no entry for the current
release. It is also the link a CRAN reader follows.

The root `CHANGELOG.md` is the source of truth for this repository, and `NEWS.md` mirrors it for
CRAN. The mirror has fallen behind. Copying the 0.2.0 section across fixes the page and the link.

title: Decide whether igv() and gosling() ship in R
description:
The R package ships 15 components. Python and JavaScript ship 17. The two missing from R are
`igv()` and `gosling()`.

Two files promise this changes:

- `pkg-r/README.md` says both "stayed out of this CRAN release to keep the installed package under
  CRAN's 5 MB limit, and a later release adds them back to R".
- `docs/index.html` says "the genome-browser pair (igv.js and Gosling) ships in R from r-universe
  until a later release adds them to CRAN".

The second claim is wrong. r-universe builds from `pkg-r/`, which has no igv or gosling source, no
NAMESPACE entry and no man page. The r-universe API returns 50 exports and none of them match. An R
user who follows that sentence installs from r-universe and still has 15 components.

The prose in both files is being corrected to say what is true today: R has 15, the other two
languages have 17.

What is left to decide is whether R gets them at all. Either ship them and say so, or drop the
promise. The 5 MB limit is the constraint to work against.

title: The CRAN downloads badge URL is missing its period segment
description:
`pkg-r/README.md` carries:

```markdown
[![CRAN downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/plotomics)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=plotomics)
```

cranlogs expects `/badges/<period>/<package>`. With the period left out, `plotomics` lands in the period slot and the badge renders a number that means nothing.

Valid periods are `last-day`, `last-week`, `last-month` and `grand-total`. `usethis::use_cran_badge()` emits the `grand-total` form:

```markdown
[![CRAN downloads](https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/grand-total/plotomics)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=plotomics)
```

plotomics is on CRAN at 0.1.0, published 2026-09-04, with real download numbers, so the badge has something true to show once the URL is right.

title: Publish the JavaScript API docs at /plotomics/js/
description:
The docs hub has a door for R and one for Python. There is none for JavaScript, and npm is the primary registry for this package.

```
https://www.samuelbharti.com/plotomics/       200
https://www.samuelbharti.com/plotomics/r/     200
https://www.samuelbharti.com/plotomics/py/    200
https://www.samuelbharti.com/plotomics/js/    404
```

`docs.yml` builds `site/py` with pdoc and `site/r` with pkgdown. No JavaScript reference is generated at all, and there is no TypeDoc configuration in the repository.

`pkg-js/README.md` also carries no badges, even though npmjs.com renders that file as the package page.

## What this needs

1. Add a TypeDoc configuration to `pkg-js`, generating into a `site` directory.
2. Add a build step to `docs.yml` and copy the output to `site/js`.
3. Link the JavaScript door from `docs/index.html`, next to the R and Python ones.
4. Point `homepage` in `pkg-js/package.json` at the new page. It currently points at the repository README.

biobouncer is the working example. It builds R with pkgdown, Python with MkDocs and JavaScript with TypeDoc, assembles all three under one landing page, and each language site links back to the other two.

title: The genome browser components have no tests
description:
Nothing exercises the Gosling and igv.js components. `pkg-js` has 19 test files and none of them touch either one.

This is what let three dependency pull requests look mergeable when they were not. #62, #63 and #65 each force-resolved gosling.js and higlass onto a peer version those libraries do not accept, and every one passed `typecheck` and `test`, because the passing tests cover the parts that do not use them.

A green run on this repository currently means the components that do not use pixi or gosling still work.

These are also the two components that ship from r-universe rather than CRAN, so they are the least exercised part of the package in every other way too.

## Options

Rendering is hard to assert on, so full coverage may not be the right target. Something is still better than nothing:

- A smoke test that mounts each component and asserts it renders without throwing. This alone would have failed the three closed pull requests.
- A snapshot of the produced DOM or canvas dimensions, to catch a component that silently stops drawing.
- If neither is worth the effort, say so in the README, so a reader knows these two carry less assurance than the rest.

The first option is the one that pays for itself, because it turns a dependency upgrade from a guess into a check.

## Related

#72 upgrades gosling.js and higlass, and needs this to be verifiable.

title: Upgrade gosling.js and higlass to unblock three held majors
description:
`pixi.js`, `react` and `react-dom` are all held at their current major in `.github/dependabot.yml`. One piece of work releases all three.

Nothing in `pkg-js/src` imports any of them. They are optional peer dependencies, declared because gosling.js and higlass need them, and those two cap every one:

```
gosling.js@1.0.7   pixi.js ^6.3.0
                   react, react-dom ^16.6.3 || ^17.0.0 || ^18.0.0
higlass@1.13.6     pixi.js ^5.0.3 || ^6.5.2
                   react, react-dom ^16.6.3 || ^17.0.0 || ^18.0.0
```

Bumping any of them without upgrading these two libraries force-resolves gosling and higlass against a version they do not support. pnpm allows it, because a peer mismatch is a warning rather than an error, so the lockfile changes and CI stays green. #62, #63 and #65 were all closed for this.

## What this needs

1. Check whether a gosling.js release supports pixi 8 and react 19. gosling 1.x is built on pixi 6.
2. Upgrade gosling.js and higlass together. higlass is a gosling dependency, so their versions move as a pair.
3. Raise `peerDependencies` in `pkg-js/package.json` to match what the new versions accept.
4. Remove the matching entries from the `ignore` list in `.github/dependabot.yml`.
5. Move `react` and `react-dom` in the same change. They share a major and break at runtime if they diverge.

## Blocked by

Test coverage for the genome browser components. Without it, nothing verifies that the upgrade works, which is the same gap that let three bad pull requests look mergeable.

title: network(): support directed edges and arrowheads
description:
`network()` builds an undirected graph, so a directed edge set is drawn without
arrowheads and the direction is lost.

## What happens

```js
let e = new P({ multi: !1, type: "undirected" });
```

The R side takes `source` and `target` columns, which read as directed, and
draws them as plain lines.

## Why it matters

Half the graphs worth drawing are directed. "FBN1 causes Marfan syndrome" and
"Marfan syndrome causes FBN1" are not the same claim, and the second one is
nonsense, but the picture cannot tell them apart. The data carries the
direction, the renderer discards it.

## Suggested fix

`type: "directed"` plus sigma's arrow edge program:

```js
import { EdgeArrowProgram } from "sigma/rendering";
// …
new Sigma(graph, container, {
  defaultEdgeType: "arrow",
  edgeProgramClasses: { arrow: EdgeArrowProgram }
});
```

Best as an option rather than a change of default, since an undirected graph
drawn with arrowheads is worse than the current behaviour. Something like
`directed = FALSE` on the R side, defaulting to what it does today.

Note this interacts with the parallel edge dropping in the silent drops issue:
under `type: "directed"`, `hasEdge(a, b)` stops matching `b -> a`, so an A to B
and a B to A pair would both survive where today the second is discarded.

## Version

Checked against the installed build at
`plotomics/htmlwidgets/lib/plotomics/network.js`.

title: network(): allow a per edge colour
description:
`network()` takes one `default_edge_color` for the whole graph and no per edge
colour, so edges that mean different things have to be drawn identically.

## What happens

The R signature offers `default_edge_color` and nothing else for edge
appearance. In the builder, every edge is created with the same colour:

```js
e.addEdge(f.source, f.target, {
  color: i.defaultEdgeColor,
  ...(f.weight !== void 0 ? { weight: f.weight, size: f.weight } : {})
});
```

`weight` is the one per edge property that gets through, and it maps to edge
size, so width is already variable per edge. Colour is not.

## Why it matters

In a knowledge graph an edge can be an assertion or a denial of that assertion.
Drawing a negation the same as the claim it denies does not omit information, it
states the opposite of the source. We currently have to declare that the canvas
cannot show negation at all and push the user to a table to find out.

The general case is any graph where edge type carries meaning: activates versus
inhibits, upstream versus downstream, high confidence versus low.

## Suggested fix

Read an optional `color` column off the edge data frame, the same way `weight`
is read now, and fall back to `defaultEdgeColor` when it is absent:

```js
color: f.color ?? i.defaultEdgeColor
```

That is a one line change in the builder plus a column in the R side, and it
covers most of the need. A dashed or dotted option would cover the rest, though
sigma needs a custom edge program for that, so it is a bigger ask and probably
belongs in its own issue.

## Version

Checked against the installed build at
`plotomics/htmlwidgets/lib/plotomics/network.js`.

title: network(): report the edges it drops instead of dropping them silently
description:
`network()` drops edges silently: self loops, second copies of a pair, and
edges whose endpoints are not in the node table all disappear before anything
is drawn, with no count reported anywhere.

## What happens

The graph is built as a simple undirected graph:

```js
let e = new P({ multi: !1, type: "undirected" });
```

and the edge loop is:

```js
for (let f of edges(n))
  !e.hasNode(f.source) || !e.hasNode(f.target) ||
    (f.source !== f.target &&
      (e.hasEdge(f.source, f.target) ||
        e.addEdge(f.source, f.target, { color: i.defaultEdgeColor, … })));
```

Three drops, none of them announced:

1. an endpoint missing from the node table
2. `f.source === f.target`, so no self loops
3. `e.hasEdge(source, target)` already true, so only the first edge between any
   pair survives

## Why it matters

A picture missing a fifth of its edges looks exactly like a complete one. The
caller passed 268 edges and got 262 drawn, and nothing in the return value or
the console says so, so there is no way to tell the user what they are not
looking at.

This is not a request to draw them. `multi: false` is a defensible choice for a
WebGL renderer and self loops are genuinely awkward. The ask is that the drops
be visible.

## Suggested fix

Cheapest useful version: return the counts on the instance, or emit them once
on render, so a caller can report them.

```js
{ dropped: { danglingEndpoint: 3, selfLoops: 0, parallelEdges: 6 } }
```

A `console.warn` when any count is non zero would already be an improvement on
silence.

If parallel edges are ever wanted, `multi: true` plus a curvature program is the
sigma-side answer, but that is a much larger change and probably a separate
issue.

## Version

Checked against the installed build at
`plotomics/htmlwidgets/lib/plotomics/network.js`.

title: network(): emit node clicks to Shiny
description:
`network()` never reports a node click to Shiny, so no Shiny app can drive a
detail panel from the canvas.

## What happens

The widget builds a Shiny options wrapper that would post the selection:

```js
function Yr(n, i) {
  let e = window;
  return e.HTMLWidgets?.shinyMode && e.Shiny?.setInputValue && n.id
    ? { ...i, onSelect: t => e.Shiny?.setInputValue?.(`${n.id}_selected`, t, { priority: "event" }) }
    : i;
}
```

`onSelect` appears exactly once in the built bundle, in that definition. The
network component never calls it. It binds two sigma events and no more:

```js
u.on("enterNode", ({ node: p }) => { … })   // highlight neighbours, show tooltip
u.on("leaveNode", () => { … })
```

So `input$<id>_selected` is never set, and a click on the canvas reaches
nothing.

## Why it matters

A network is usually the index into something else: click an entity, see its
detail. Without a click event the widget can only be looked at. In our case
(a knowledge graph viewer) the inspector panel beside the canvas had no way of
ever being filled, and we had to make a table the selection mechanism instead.

The heatmap and volcano widgets look like they have the same shared helper
available, so this may be worth checking across the family rather than only in
`network`.

## Suggested fix

```js
u.on("clickNode", ({ node }) => opts.onSelect?.(node));
u.on("clickStage", () => opts.onSelect?.(null));
```

`clickStage` clearing the selection matters as much as setting it: without it a
selection can only ever be replaced, never dismissed.

Worth considering whether the payload should be the node key alone or an object
with the key, group and coordinates. The key alone is enough for our use and is
the smaller commitment.

## Version

Checked against the installed build at
`plotomics/htmlwidgets/lib/plotomics/network.js`.
